t: The One Thing You Must Do To Avoid Stress And Improve Behavior improve-behavior/
q: Because every one of the hundreds of teachers I’ve given this advice to—through my coaching practice and personal mentoring—has experienced a dramatic decrease in stress.
If not for this strategy, I don’t think I could have become a teacher—or stayed one for long.
It’s to never again try to convince students to behave. It’s to refrain from pulling them aside for lectures, pep-talks, and counseling sessions.
You see, all that extra attention communicates to students just how much their behavior means to you, which effectively shifts the leverage and control in the relationship over to them.
You let your classroom management plan do the heavy lifting for you. You rely on it exclusively. You fulfill your promise to follow it exactly as it’s written.
They’ll develop a strong, intrinsic desire to behave. Naturally and all on their own.

t: 25 Classroom Management Myths To Ponder This Summer summer/
q: It occurred to me while responding to a recent flurry of emails just how prevalent the myths are surrounding classroom management.
They're held on to tightly, often reverently, by those who seek to justify their struggles.
So I present the 25 most common myths in the bright light of day.
My hope is that this list will help you identify those areas in need of improvement.
Individually, the myths may require further explanation, especially if you’re new to our website.
It’s important to periodically take a step back and gain some perspective, to reflect on where you are now and where you’d like to be.

t: How To Reignite Your Love Of Teaching
q: It’s official. A culture of pressure and stress has infected the teaching profession. It’s palpable in school after school and district after district.

Much of the stress teachers experience is due to things beyond their control. If it’s something you must do, like a mandate from administration, then it’s self-sabotage to get worked up about it—or even give it a second thought.
Teachers who struggle the most with stress and dissatisfaction assume that very little is within their control.
When you focus on enjoying your students, when you savor the relationships, the connections, and the act of teaching them, all that other stuff you're preoccupied with will fade away.

I hear from frustrated teachers every day who believe that they’re boxed in and have no options. But in every case, they’re upset over things that are either completely under their control or needn’t have any affect on enjoying their job.

It may not be as easy being a teacher as it once was, even five years ago. But with the right attitude and classroom management approach, and a healthy dose of shrewdness, it can be every bit as fun and rewarding.

t: Should You Hold Students Accountable On The Last Day Of School? https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/06/03/hold-students-accountable-the-last-day-of-school/
q: The most important reason is because you made a promise. You said you would follow through every time a class rule was broken. So just for the sake of integrity, it's worth doing.
You see, when you fail to follow your classroom management plan through to the end, you’re telling them that it was all a sham, that you didn’t really mean what you said—not entirely anyway.
For many, their memory of you—the lessons you taught them and the truth and honor you displayed—will keep them afloat through difficult times in their life.
It’s much easier to be consistent when you allow yourself zero wiggle room. Decisions become automatic. Doubt is removed. Stress is all but eliminated.
They’re an opportunity to make the right choice and become not just another teacher . . . But a leader whose example stays with students for the rest of their lives.
